name: <header>
description: Represents introductory content for its nearest ancestor — page title and nav for the page, or a heading/byline for an <article>.
notes: Unlike a <div class="header">, screen readers can jump straight to it as a landmark region.

name: <nav>
description: Marks a block of major navigation links, such as a site's main menu or breadcrumbs.
notes: Reserve it for primary navigation blocks — not every group of links needs to be a <nav>.

name: <main>
description: Identifies the dominant, unique content of the document, excluding repeated elements like headers, footers and sidebars.
notes: Should appear exactly once per page and lets screen reader users skip straight to the primary content.

name: <article>
description: Represents a self-contained piece of content that would make sense distributed or syndicated on its own, like a blog post, news story or forum comment.
notes: The test: if you could pull this out and reuse it elsewhere and it would still make sense, it's an <article>.

name: <section>
description: Groups a thematically related chunk of content, typically with its own heading, that forms a distinct part of the page.
notes: Unlike <div>, a <section> implies the content is a distinct, headed thematic group — not just a styling wrapper.

name: <aside>
description: Represents content tangentially related to the surrounding content, such as a sidebar, pull quote or ad block.
notes: Content could be removed without reducing the meaning of the main content around it.

name: <footer>
description: Represents footer content for its nearest ancestor — copyright, contact links or related documents for the page, or metadata for an <article>.

name: <figure>
description: Groups self-contained content — usually an image, diagram or code snippet — together with an optional caption, as a single referenceable unit.
notes:
Semantically ties an image to its caption, unlike a plain

name: <figcaption>
description: Provides a caption or legend describing the contents of its parent <figure>.
notes: Can appear as the first or last child of <figure>.

name: <time>
description: Marks up a human-readable date or time while also providing a machine-readable equivalent for browsers and search engines.
notes: Unlike a plain <span>, it lets tools reliably parse and index the date regardless of how it's displayed.

name: <mark>
description: Highlights text that is relevant or noteworthy in the current context, such as a search term match.
notes: Conveys relevance, unlike <span class="highlight"> which carries no meaning without CSS.

name: <address>
description: Provides contact information for the nearest <article> or the page's author/owner — a person, organization or email, not a postal address specifically.
notes: Despite the name, it's for authorship/contact info, not for marking up arbitrary street addresses.

name: <details>
description: Creates a native, collapsible disclosure widget that the user can toggle open or closed, with no JavaScript required.
notes: Replaces the common pattern of a button plus JS-toggled div for simple show/hide UI.

name: <summary>
description: Defines the always-visible label/heading for a <details> disclosure widget; clicking it toggles the widget open or closed.
notes: Must be the first child of <details>; only one <summary> is used per <details>.

name: <search>
description: Identifies a section containing search or filtering controls for the current page or site, as a distinct landmark region.
notes: A newer semantic landmark — before it existed, a <form role="search"> was the common substitute.
